lead: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is a three-layer device in which a small base current controls a much larger collector current. That is why it behaves as a current-controlled current source. Two junctions share the middle layer: one is forward biased, the other reverse biased, and charge carriers flow from emitter to collector. The same idea gives amplification in audio and radio circuits and fast switching in inverters and logic. NPN and PNP are the two polarities. It is also called a bipolar transistor, or simply a transistor.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the diode-like base-emitter junction, and Unit 1 for KVL and load lines.

blocks.text: An NPN transistor has three regions: emitter, base, collector. The emitter is heavily doped with n-type silicon. The base is a thin, lightly doped p-type layer. The collector is a larger n-type region that collects carriers and dissipates heat. A PNP transistor swaps every polarity.

Two junctions exist. The base-emitter (BE) junction is forward biased at about 0.7 V for silicon. The collector-base (CB) junction is reverse biased. In this active mode the emitter pushes electrons into the thin base. Few electrons recombine with holes there; most are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased CB junction. The small recombination current is the base current I<sub>B</sub>, and the large swept current is the collector current I<sub>C</sub>.

blocks.where: I<sub>E</sub> is emitter current, I<sub>B</sub> is base current and I<sub>C</sub> is collector current, all in amperes (A).

blocks.text: Two ratios describe the device. α = I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>E</sub> is the common-base current gain; it lies between 0.95 and 0.99. β = I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>B</sub> is the common-emitter current gain; it lies between 50 and 300. They are linked by β = α/(1 − α).

blocks.where: α is the fraction of emitter current that reaches the collector, and β is the collector-to-base current ratio. Both are pure numbers.

sections.h3: Regions, biasing and the load line

blocks.text: Three regions appear on the output curves. In cut-off the BE junction is not forward biased, I<sub>B</sub> is zero and I<sub>C</sub> is only leakage. In the active region BE is forward biased and CB is reverse biased; I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub>. In saturation both junctions are forward biased and I<sub>C</sub> is set by the external resistor, not by β.

Biasing fixes a steady base current and collector voltage. Four common methods: fixed base uses one resistor from V<sub>CC</sub> to base; collector-to-base feedback connects a resistor from collector to base; voltage divider holds the base voltage with two resistors; emitter bias adds a resistor in the emitter to steady the current. The first is simple but β-sensitive. The last two are preferred when β varies.
I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/R<sub>B</sub>,   I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub>,   V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>R<sub>C</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>CC</sub> is supply voltage in volts, V<sub>BE</sub> ≈ 0.7 V, R<sub>B</sub> is base resistor in ohms, R<sub>C</sub> is collector resistor in ohms, and V<sub>CE</sub> is collector-emitter voltage in volts.

blocks.text: The dc load line is the line V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>R<sub>C</sub> drawn on the output curves. Its ends are cut-off (I<sub>C</sub> = 0, V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub>) and saturation (V<sub>CE</sub> ≈ 0.2 V, I<sub>C</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − 0.2)/R<sub>C</sub>). The Q-point is where the chosen I<sub>B</sub> curve crosses the load line.

The common-emitter (CE) connection uses the emitter as the common terminal. Its input characteristic plots I<sub>B</sub> against V<sub>BE</sub> for a fixed V<sub>CE</sub>. It looks like a diode curve: I<sub>B</sub> is almost zero below about 0.6 V and rises steeply after 0.7 V.

The CE output characteristic plots I<sub>C</sub> against V<sub>CE</sub> for fixed I<sub>B</sub>. Near V<sub>CE</sub> = 0 the curve rises steeply: this is saturation. Above about 0.2 V the curve is almost flat: this is the active region, where I<sub>C</sub> ≈ βI<sub>B</sub>. The flat part has a slight upward slope because a higher V<sub>CE</sub> widens the collector depletion layer and narrows the base, so β rises a little. At very high V<sub>CE</sub> breakdown occurs. The figure plots three curves for I<sub>B</sub> = 20 µA, 40 µA and 60 µA.

The common-base (CB) connection uses the base as the common terminal. Its input characteristic plots I<sub>E</sub> against V<sub>EB</sub> at fixed V<sub>CB</sub>, again a diode curve. Its output characteristic plots I<sub>C</sub> against V<sub>CB</sub> at fixed I<sub>E</sub>. That curve is even flatter than the CE curve, because I<sub>C</sub> = αI<sub>E</sub> and α is close to 1. The CB current gain is below 1, but the CB connection has low input impedance and is used in high-frequency circuits.

figure.caption: CE output curves for an NPN transistor at three base currents. Notice the steep saturation rise near 0 V and the nearly flat active region above about 0.2 V.

spec.aria: Plot of CE output characteristics for an NPN transistor: each base current gives a curve that rises steeply near zero VCE and then stays almost flat as VCE increases.

examples.question: A fixed-base NPN circuit has V<sub>CC</sub> = 12 V, R<sub>B</sub> = 470 kΩ, R<sub>C</sub> = 2.2 kΩ, β = 100 and V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V. Find I<sub>B</sub>, I<sub>C</sub> and V<sub>CE</sub>, and state the region.
steps: Write the base loop: V<sub>CC</sub> = I<sub>B</sub>R<sub>B</sub> + V<sub>BE</sub>. So I<sub>B</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>)/R<sub>B</sub>.
Assume active region: I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub> = 100 × 24.0 µA = 2400 µA = 2.40 mA.
Collector loop: V<sub>CE</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub> − I<sub>C</sub>R<sub>C</sub> = 12 V − (2.40 mA × 2.2 kΩ). 2.40 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 5.28 V. So V<sub>CE</sub> = 6.72 V ≈ 6.7 V.

Check saturation: I<sub>C(sat)</sub> ≈ V<sub>CC</sub>/R<sub>C</sub> = 12 V/2.2 kΩ = 5.45 mA. The calculated 2.40 mA is below 5.45 mA, and V<sub>CE</sub> = 6.7 V is well above 0.2 V. The active-region assumption is correct.
examples.answer: I<sub>B</sub> = 24.0 µA, I<sub>C</sub> = 2.40 mA, V<sub>CE</sub> = 6.7 V, so the transistor is in the active region.
examples.check:
VCC = 12.0
RB = 470e3
RC = 2.2e3
beta = 100
VBE = 0.7
IB = (VCC - VBE) / RB
IC = beta * IB
VCE = VCC - IC * RC
ICsat = VCC / RC
print(f"{IB*1e6:.1f}")
print(f"{IC*1e3:.2f}")
print(f"{VCE:.1f}")
print(f"{ICsat*1e3:.2f}")

traps: Do not use I<sub>C</sub> = βI<sub>B</sub> before checking the region. It holds only while V<sub>CE</sub> is above about 0.2 V. If the calculated V<sub>CE</sub> falls below that, the transistor is saturated and I<sub>C</sub> = (V<sub>CC</sub> − 0.2)/R<sub>C</sub>.
Do not swap α and β. α = I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>E</sub> is below 1; β = I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>B</sub> is usually 50 to 300.
Subtract V<sub>BE</sub> before dividing by R<sub>B</sub>. Using I<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>CC</sub>/R<sub>B</sub> overestimates the base current.
In the CE output curve, the steep part near the origin is saturation, not cut-off. Cut-off is the bottom curve where I<sub>B</sub> = 0.
Keep kΩ and mA consistent: mA × kΩ gives volts. Mixing ohms and milliamperes gives a factor-of-1000 error.

quiz.q: State the doping and thickness of the emitter, base and collector of an NPN BJT.
quiz.a: Emitter: heavily doped n-type. Base: thin, lightly doped p-type. Collector: larger n-type region, moderately doped.

quiz.q: Why does a thin, lightly doped base make β large?
quiz.a: Most emitter electrons cross the base without recombining, so I<sub>B</sub> is small while I<sub>C</sub> is almost equal to I<sub>E</sub>. Since β = I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>B</sub>, a small I<sub>B</sub> gives a large β.

quiz.q: A BJT has α = 0.98 and I<sub>E</sub> = 5 mA. Find β, I<sub>C</sub> and I<sub>B</sub>.
quiz.a: β = α/(1 − α) = 0.98/0.02 = 49. I<sub>C</sub> = αI<sub>E</sub> = 0.98 × 5 mA = 4.9 mA. I<sub>B</sub> = I<sub>E</sub> − I<sub>C</sub> = 0.1 mA.

quiz.q: A fixed-base NPN circuit has V<sub>CC</sub> = 10 V, R<sub>B</sub> = 1 MΩ, R<sub>C</sub> = 1 kΩ, β = 150 and V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V. Find I<sub>B</sub>, I<sub>C</sub>, V<sub>CE</sub> and the region.
quiz.a: I<sub>B</sub> = (10 − 0.7)/1 MΩ = 9.3 µA. I<sub>C</sub> = 150 × 9.3 µA = 1.395 mA. V<sub>CE</sub> = 10 − 1.395 mA × 1 kΩ = 8.605 V. I<sub>C(sat)</sub> = 10 mA, so the transistor is active.

quiz.q: Why is the active part of the CE output curve not perfectly horizontal?
quiz.a: Increasing V<sub>CE</sub> increases the reverse bias of the CB junction. Its depletion layer widens into the thin base, reducing base recombination. I<sub>C</sub> rises slightly for the same I<sub>B</sub>; this is base-width modulation, or the Early effect.

quiz.q: A fixed-base circuit is designed with β = 100 and sits at V<sub>CE</sub> = 5 V. The transistor is replaced by one with β = 300. What happens to I<sub>B</sub>, I<sub>C</sub> and V<sub>CE</sub>?
quiz.a: I<sub>B</sub> stays the same because it is set by V<sub>CC</sub>, V<sub>BE</sub> and R<sub>B</sub>. The circuit tries to make I<sub>C</sub> three times larger, but the collector resistor limits it. The transistor moves into saturation, I<sub>C</sub> ≈ (V<sub>CC</sub> − 0.2)/R<sub>C</sub>, and V<sub>CE</sub> falls to about 0.2 V.

quiz.q: Why is the CB output characteristic flatter than the CE output characteristic?
quiz.a: In CB, I<sub>C</sub> = αI<sub>E</sub> with I<sub>E</sub> fixed and α close to 1, so I<sub>C</sub> barely changes with V<sub>CB</sub>. In CE, the base current is fixed, but V<sub>CE</sub> changes the base width and β slightly, so I<sub>C</sub> changes a little more.

beyond: Not for the exam. BJTs remain in analog ICs as gain stages, in power circuits as switches, and in bandgap voltage references. BiCMOS chips combine bipolar speed with CMOS logic. The IGBT is a BJT output stage driven by a MOSFET input. Silicon-germanium heterojunction BJTs work at microwave frequencies in phone radios. Search next for the Early effect, the Ebers-Moll model, the Gummel-Poon model and the transit frequency f<sub>T</sub>.
